Gopika called Arnab at eleven at night from outside the group's hostel in Salt Lake. She had one bag. 'Can I come to you? Just for tonight.'
He was there in forty minutes in a borrowed car. He didn't ask why. He didn't say I told you so.
On the drive she talked in pieces. The promised job at the group's school had never come, after three years. She was so tired she'd fallen asleep standing in the prayer hall. And Arnab had kept sending her cricket scores every Sunday, no matter what.
The next weeks were practical. He cleared the spare room. He helped her write a CV that didn't have a three-year hole in it, and forwarded two openings from his office. When she couldn't decide what to eat without asking someone, he found a counsellor who worked with people leaving such groups and went with her to the first appointment.
He never once said the group's name with a sneer.

qa.q: How long did it take Arnab to arrive?
qa.a: He was there in forty minutes in a borrowed car.

qa.q: What does Gopika's trouble deciding what to eat suggest about her state?
qa.a: It suggests the group had taken over her choices for so long that she has lost confidence in her own judgement.

qa.q: Which kinds of support from Arnab made leaving possible and safe?
qa.a: No blame, patient listening, a room to stay in, help with her CV and job openings, and going with her to a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt, sending cricket scores every Sunday with no reply for years?
qa.a: He may have felt worried and sometimes hopeless, but kept going because he wanted her to know someone outside still cared.

grounding: It shows a young woman leaving after a broken promise and exhaustion, supported by a trusted friend with no blame, practical help and counselling.

'Nitin? It's past midnight. Where are you?'
'Bus stand. Near the flyover.' His voice cracked. 'I left, Hafsa. I just walked out.'
'Stay there. I'm coming.'
Twenty minutes later she found him on a bench, shoes untied, a plastic bag of clothes on his lap.
'I'm so tired,' he said. 'Five years. They said the new centre would be ours. It went to the leader's cousin.'
'You don't have to explain now.'
'You kept messaging. Even when I told you to stop.'
'I know.'
'Aren't you going to say you were right?'
'No.' She sat beside him. 'You can sleep at my aunt's place tonight. She has a spare room. Tomorrow we'll sort out your phone and ID.'
'I don't have a job. I don't know what I think about anything.'
'That's okay. There are counsellors who help with exactly this. We'll go together.'
Nitin leaned forward, head in his hands, and breathed.

qa.a: She found him on a bench at the bus stand, near the flyover.

I left on a Tuesday, and not in a dramatic way. I was just too tired. Four years of 4 a.m. starts, and the leader had broken his promise, again, about the house we'd all share. I sat on my bunk and couldn't stand up.
I texted one person: Leela, my school friend, who had kept sending me birthday messages every year even when I didn't reply. "Can I come?"
She didn't say I told you so. She picked me up from the bus stand, made rajma chawal and let me sleep for fourteen hours. Then she helped with the boring things: a new SIM, my old bank account, a bed in a working women's hostel, a CV that explained the gap.
She also found me a counsellor. It took months before I could make a decision without asking myself what the leader would think. I'm Disha, and my first decision of my own was the colour of my hostel curtains.

qa.q: What did Leela make when Disha arrived?
qa.a: Rajma chawal.

qa.q: How did Disha feel on the day of leaving?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and let down, so drained by broken promises that she couldn't stand up.

qa.q: Which kinds of support from Leela helped most?
qa.a: No blame, food and rest, practical help with a SIM, bank, hostel bed and CV, and finding a counsellor to rebuild her own thinking.

qa.q: What might Leela have felt picking Disha up at the bus stand?
qa.a: Leela was probably relieved and emotional, glad her yearly messages had kept a door open.

grounding: A young woman leaves a group out of exhaustion and a broken promise, and a trusted friend helps without blame, with practical steps and counselling.

Counsellor's note, first session
Afreen left a high-control group three weeks ago after nearly two years. She said it began to end when a promise to members about "shared savings" turned out to be false, and her old manager, Harish, messaged out of the blue to ask how she was. That message, she said, was the first time in months someone outside had written without judging.
She is exhausted, sleeps badly and apologises often. She kept asking if she was stupid. I told her plainly that leaving took courage and that none of this made her stupid.
Practical steps agreed today: she will stay with her aunt for now; Harish has offered her part-time work at her old office from next month; I will help her apply for a replacement ID card, which the group kept.
Therapy goal: to practise making small decisions on her own again. We will meet weekly.

qa.q: Who messaged Afreen out of the blue?
qa.a: Her old manager, Harish.

qa.q: What does Afreen asking if she was stupid reveal?
qa.a: She feels ashamed and exhausted, blaming herself for having been drawn in.

qa.q: Which steps in the plan support her recovery, and why?
qa.a: Staying with her aunt, part-time work, a new ID and weekly counselling, because they give safety, income and space to rebuild independent choices.

qa.q: What might Harish have felt when Afreen replied?
qa.a: Harish was likely relieved and glad that a simple, non-judging message had reached her.

grounding: A counsellor records a young woman's exit after a broken promise and a trusted contact, with no blame, practical help and counselling.

Saturday
Chandrika is sleeping in my room now. She arrived at midnight with one bag and no phone; the group kept it. She said, "I'm sorry, I didn't know where else to go," and I said, "This is exactly where to go."
She's so tired. She told me the leader had promised her a job in the group's school, and it never came, and when she asked, they called her ungrateful. That was the end for her.
I didn't ask why she stayed so long. I remembered what the helpline person told me last year: no blame, just listen. So I listened, and made khichdi.
Tomorrow: buy her a basic phone, call her mother together if she wants, ask my manager about the receptionist vacancy. Monday: find a counsellor who understands groups like this.
She laughed once tonight, at my cat. First time in two years I've heard it.
Pema

qa.q: What did Pema make for Chandrika?
qa.a: Khichdi.

qa.q: What did Pema feel when Chandrika laughed at the cat?
qa.a: Pema felt moved and hopeful, hearing a friend laugh for the first time in two years.

qa.q: Which items on Pema's plan matter most, and why?
qa.a: A phone, a call to her mother, a job lead and a counsellor, because practical help and professional support rebuild independence.

qa.q: How was Chandrika feeling when she arrived at midnight?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and ashamed, apologising, after a broken promise and being called ungrateful.

grounding: A friend takes in a young woman leaving a group, listening without blame and planning practical help and counselling.
